newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bildt hopes for concrete steps on war criminals.
newsitem.headline: Bildt hopes for concrete steps on war criminals.

text.p: The international community's top official in Bosnia, Carl Bildt, hopes for a concrete action plan to secure the arrest of indicted war criminals, his spokesman said on Thursday.

"He (Bildt) would like to see urgent planning that addresses this concern so that something concrete is done and words are translated into action," said Colum Murphy, when asked what Bildt would consider a successful end to the London conference.

Foreign ministers from North America, Europe and the Balkans are winding up a two-day conference reviewing Bosnia's first year of peace, at which the failure to apprehend dozens of war criminals has topped the agenda.

But Murphy held out little hope that the London meeting would produce measures strong enough to force Croatia, Yugoslavia and Bosnia's Croats and Serbs to hand over the indictees living in their midst.

"Bildt is asking his constituents in London for more action. They have agreed to give him greater powers of economic coordination and he can bang the table but in the end power resides in the various capitals," said Murphy.
"What you are talking about is the state of international relations at the moment. It should be a lot better of course."
Only seven of the 74 men indicted for their role in the bloody wars that accompanied the break-up of old Yugoslavia are in the custody of the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague.
Many are in territory controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, who have refused to hand over their former president Radovan Karadzic and ex-military chief Ratko Mladic.

It is currently the responsibility of local authorities to arrest war criminals, but only Bosnia's Moslems have done so. The threat of sanctions and economic penalties has had little effect on the others.

Britain's cold response to calls for the thousands of well- armed NATO troops in Bosnia to seek out war criminals and its downgrading of the Tribunal to observer status in London indicate its wish to push the issue onto the back-burner.
Canada has raised its voice to support Bildt, while the United States has said more must be done but has ruled out permitting NATO to take military action.

NATO has said since it began its peace mission a year ago that it has no mandate to hunt down war criminals. It has been accused of turning a blind eye to indictees roaming at will across Bosnia rather than risk an incident with casualties.

Murphy said Bildt had suggested creating a special police force capable of arresting war criminals but the idea had not got much further than "the corridors and quiet margins of diplomatic conferences."
